descriptors.evidence: Highest occurrence count of all 36 fields (57,110) and 99.96% numeric-parseable with very short values (mean 2.95 chars) like '.02', '.1', '.2024', '.25' -- the same fractional-decimal profile as dim_a/b/c and load_rating. The generic 'item_spec_7' name (one of presumably many numbered spec slots) gives no clue to the real-world quantity it holds, so the numeric role is solid but the concrete meaning is genuinely unclear.

99.93% numeric-parseable, short bare-decimal values ('.5','.66','0','0.1'), 2734 distinct values over 46,687 rows -- the classic profile of a physical dimension component (width/depth/height) stored without units. Grouped with dim_b/dim_c of near-identical stat shape, suggesting a 3-axis dimension triple, though which specific axis 'a' denotes is not recoverable from the name alone.

99.99% numeric-parseable, bare-decimal values ('.5','0','0.04','0.08'), 2604 distinct over 37,136 rows -- same dimension-component profile as dim_a/dim_c, most likely a second axis (e.g. depth) of a length/width/height triple, though the specific axis identity cannot be confirmed from name/samples alone.

100% numeric-parseable (no empty-string sample, unlike dim_a/b), values like '.2','.375','.5','.625','.75' -- quarter/eighth-inch fraction increments typical of furniture dimension listings; completes the likely 3-axis dimension group with dim_a/dim_b.

Name directly signals a weight/load capacity value and the field is 99.97% numeric-parseable. However the visible low-end samples (0, 0.01, 0.2, 0.22, 0.5) look implausibly small for a furniture weight rating (normally tens-to-hundreds of lbs); these are most likely just the ascending-sort low tail of a wider distribution rather than the field's typical values, so I trust the name but flag the sample mismatch.

Only 83 distinct values over 8,602 occurrences with round-number samples (0, 1, 10, 100) resembling an internal score/index/tier rather than a physical measurement. The generic name 'prep_index' does not map to any confident real-world merchandising concept (assembly-prep steps? priority score?), so while the numeric role is clear, the semantic meaning is genuinely uncertain and unlikely to be something a shopper searches on directly.

Exactly 2 distinct values ('no'/'yes'), 0% numeric-parseable, mean length 2.25 (between 'no'=2 and 'yes'=3 chars) -- an unambiguous binary flag. The anonymized 'flag_12' name gives no indication which specific product feature (assembly, pet-safety, outdoor-use, etc.) it represents, so I can't propose confident aliases.

2 distinct values ('no'/'yes'), 0% numeric-parseable, mean length 2.76 -- a clean binary flag, structurally identical to the other flag_* fields but with its own distinct occurrence count (25,258), implying it tracks a different underlying yes/no feature whose specific meaning the anonymized name does not reveal.

3 distinct values ('', 'no', 'yes') -- a yes/no flag with an additional empty/unspecified state, 0% numeric-parseable. The blank third state suggests this attribute is not always declared by merchants, which should be modeled as 'unknown' rather than false.

3 distinct values ('', 'no', 'yes'), 0% numeric-parseable, occurrence count (7,541) close to flag_14's -- same tri-state yes/no/unspecified boolean pattern; specific real-world feature not recoverable from the anonymized name.
2 distinct values ('no'/'yes'), 0% numeric-parseable, mean length 2.39 -- a clean binary flag with its own occurrence footprint (8,696), distinct from the other flag_* fields.
2 distinct values ('no'/'yes'), 0% numeric-parseable, mean length 2.51, occurs in 10,779 rows -- consistent binary-flag structure; underlying feature unknown from name alone.

3 distinct values ('', 'no', 'yes'), 0% numeric-parseable, mean length 2.6 -- another tri-state yes/no/unspecified boolean, occurring in 12,555 rows; specific feature it tracks is not identifiable from the anonymized name.

70 distinct multi-word style/theme phrases ('american traditional', 'antik', 'apothecary', 'asian inspired'), mean length 15.2 chars, low uniqueness ratio (0.0036) showing heavy reuse across 19,221 rows -- a classic decor/style taxonomy field, and style is a very common furniture search dimension.

Only 16 distinct, shorter style labels ('boho','coastal','country','country / farmhouse') versus tag_group_a's 70 finer-grained tags -- looks like a coarser/parent style category running alongside tag_group_a. The compound 'country / farmhouse' value shows some entries are themselves merged categories.

All visible samples are lowercase country names (afghanistan, argentina, australia, bahrain, bangladesh) and 71 distinct values matches a plausible country list -- unambiguously country-of-origin despite the generic 'origin_code' name.

Name implies a yes/no boolean ('flag'), but the real data has 10 distinct textual values including 'full', 'full assembly', 'full assembly needed', and 'light' -- a multi-level assembly-requirement category, not a binary flag. Trusting the data over the name here.

9 distinct wood-finish phrases ('dark brown wood', 'espresso wood', 'gray wood', 'light wood'). Notably 'esptresso wood' is a misspelled duplicate of 'espresso wood', showing the distinct-value count is inflated by data-entry noise rather than a genuine 10th finish -- a fuzzy-match/normalization concern for the fast path.

Samples are '100 % <material>' composition strings (cotton, fine porcelain, medium density fiberboard, water hyacinth); 250 distinct values but only 0.023 uniqueness shows heavy reuse -- a bounded, reused material vocabulary. Material is one of the most commonly searched furniture attributes.

Simpler material names than material_code, without percentage prefixes (acacia wood, acrylic, aluminium, aluminum) -- likely a secondary material attribute (e.g. hardware/frame vs. upholstery). Both British 'aluminium' and American 'aluminum' spellings appear as separate distinct values, a normalization defect that fragments what should be one canonical value.

Values ('abstract', 'abstract/novelty', 'amphora', 'arabesque') read as decorative shape/form descriptors, plausible for decor items like vases or mirrors rather than a numeric 'code'; 99 distinct values with low reuse (0.0109) fits a moderate-cardinality style enum, but shape/form is a less common direct search term than color or material.

Similar profile to form_code (abstract, abstract cubism, abstract/geometric) -- a design/pattern style enum. Sample '[ doesnotapply ]' is a bracketed null-sentinel value, not a real design category, and should be normalized to null rather than counted as a 94th legitimate value.

Name and several samples support 'color' as the core concept, but the data is notably contaminated: sample values include bare junk tokens ('0', ';') and an explicit meta-sentinel '[ tied to : color ]' -- the raw feed appears to literally flag this value as derived from/aliased to a separate color field. Another sample, '2 taupe , 2 teal , 2 white', is a multi-color count list for a set/kit rather than a single color. The high distinct-value count (4,686) and uniqueness (0.1782) reflect this composite/free-form contamination on top of genuine single-color values.

Despite the 'hue' name implying color, the actual samples -- acacia, acorn, acrylic, aged brass -- are materials/finishes, not color words like the taupe/teal/white seen in hue_code. This looks like a mislabeled finish/material attribute rather than a true color field; trusting the data over the name, though the exact intended concept remains uncertain.

Samples (acrylic, aged ash, aged brass) match a surface-material/finish interpretation consistent with the name. Notably near-identical sample values appear in hue_code_2, suggesting these two fields may be overlapping/duplicate finish attributes within this feed rather than fully independent concepts.

Compound composition strings ('10 % mdf/ 10 % half pu/ 10 % non-woven/ 10 % sponge/ 60 % metal frame', '100 % cotton') describing upholstery/frame material blends; 113 distinct values reused across 7,247 rows (0.0156 uniqueness) is a bounded vocabulary, though the multi-material compound values make exact-match less reliable than substring matching for shopper queries like 'cotton'.

Name suggests fabric color, and most samples support that ('2 tone espresso', '2-tone brown', '2-tone latte'), but one sample ('0354-92 ; 0354-92') is a raw manufacturer fabric SKU code repeated with a semicolon delimiter -- the field is contaminated with internal codes alongside human-readable color descriptions, which explains its unusually high uniqueness ratio (0.2978) for what should otherwise be a bounded color enum.

Only 7 distinct values despite 29,209 occurrences (0.0002 uniqueness) suggests a small enum of warranty terms ('1 year', '90 days', 'lifetime'), but one sample is a full sentence with an embedded support URL ('...please go to https://blazinwheelssupport.com/') -- customer-service boilerplate, not a comparable category, so the field mixes clean short categories with rare long free-text contamination that should probably be ignored at retrieval time.

12 distinct values including 'full', 'full warranty', 'limited', plus a duration-flavored value ('1 year limited warranty') that overlaps with coverage_duration/coverage_note -- suggests redundant, inconsistently-split warranty fields in this feed rather than one clean tier taxonomy.

112 distinct values spanning wildly inconsistent granularity -- from a bare '1' with no unit, to short phrases ('1 year'), to full sentences ('1 year from the date of purchase.', '1 year limited manufacturer warranty') -- indicating free-form entry rather than a clean structured duration field, despite low uniqueness (0.0053) showing heavy repetition of the more common phrasings.

Very high uniqueness ratio (0.9029) and long values (mean 23.06 chars) that read as artwork/print titles ('1881 oahu hawaii vintage map', 'a pelican and other birds near a pool the floating feather 1680') rather than a structured attribute. By far the lowest occurrence count of any field (546), implying it's populated only for a narrow product subset (likely wall-art/prints) -- an alternate title field for that niche category.

3,500 distinct long free-text values (mean 50.76 chars) reading as care/cleaning instructions ('wipe clean with a damp cloth', 'do not use strong liquid cleaners') -- descriptive care-instruction text, useful as a lexical-match fallback (e.g. 'machine washable') but not a structured filter facet.

Long descriptive package-contents lists (mean 27.02 chars) like '(1) stand mixer, (1) 6 quart bowl, (1) wire, (1) flat beater...' -- clearly a 'what's included' manifest. The 11.18% numeric-parseable fraction is unusual for descriptive text, suggesting some rows have bare quantity numbers or code-like fragments mixed in, another sign of inconsistent formatting.

Near-1:1 uniqueness (0.9785) over only 2,048 occurrences (far lower than most other fields, implying sparse population) with a 12-digit UPC-like sample ('069556530416') alongside manufacturer part numbers ('06.mmfpbdv.44') -- a per-item identifier. One sample, '# ref !', is a literal Excel '#REF!' formula-error string that leaked into the feed and should be treated as a corrupted/missing value, not a real code.

descriptors.relationship_semantics: Believed to hold the identifier/code of a different, related product this one is linked to (e.g. a matching, compatible, or bundled item) -- though some observed values are small integers ('1','2') that look more like a local set/kit index than a genuine external product ID, so not every value may be a true cross-product reference.
descriptors.evidence: Name explicitly signals a cross-reference to another product. Extremely low occurrence (161, one of the sparsest fields) fits an optional relationship attribute populated only where a link exists. Sample values mix tiny integers ('1','2') with larger numeric-looking codes ('140780','1795','330') -- the small integers are ambiguous between a genuine linked product ID and a local group/kit counter.

descriptors.relationship_semantics: Appears to reference the manufacturer/model code of a different but related product (e.g. a companion or paired SKU) -- the slash-separated dual-code sample suggests it may point to two linked SKUs at once, though it could alternatively be this product's own manufacturer code mislabeled as a link.
descriptors.evidence: occurrences (71) exactly equal distinct_values (71) with a perfect uniqueness_ratio of 1.0 -- every row has a unique value, consistent with a code rather than a repeated category. The sample '01-0619-884-01/01-0619-885-01' packs two slash-separated codes into one value, suggesting a reference to a pair of related SKUs (e.g. companion parts) rather than a single self-identifier, supporting the 'linked_product_code' naming.
